prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Link Inventory Audit — Q1 2025 (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Page title" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 319px
  col 2: header "URL" · longest unbreakable word 324px · one-line width 841px
  col 3: header "Last checked" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 96px
  col 4: header "Status code" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 86px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Audit page links and their latest check results for Q1 2025.","reading":"Readers identify a page by its title, inspect its URL, then compare the last-checked date and status code across rows. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.","groups":["Page title and URL identify the destination together.","Last checked and status code describe the audit result and support comparison across pages."],"keep_intact":["Status codes and dates should remain intact where possible.","URL components and page-title words should remain intact where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Page titles can wrap naturally between words.","URLs can wrap at meaningful separators; long uninterrupted segments may need splitting in narrower designs.","Headers can wrap when the corresponding data remains readable."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[100,109,82,68],"idea":"Fit the viewport, preserving room for dates and status codes while accepting substantial title and URL splitting."},{"name":"B","widths":[145,210,82,68],"idea":"Use moderate horizontal scrolling to give titles and URLs more breathing room while keeping dates and status codes intact."},{"name":"C","widths":[180,345,117,107],"idea":"Favor legibility with enough space for the longest uninterrupted URL segment and single-line audit headers, at the cost of substantial scrolling."}]}
